path: forge-ask-all.mjs --bounded --k 5, unscoped; citations via the KB's verify-citation.mjs

rows.need: I run several AI helpers at once and they keep stepping on each other or waiting blindly. How should each helper report what it's doing and pass results to the others so nothing gets lost?
I have data on who follows, replies to and shares posts from whom online. How can I find the most influential accounts and group people so my marketing push reaches the right ones?
I'm writing up requirements for a new feature and my team keeps arguing over what counts as done. How do I phrase requirements so nobody can read them two different ways?
My AI agent's long-term memory store is using too much RAM and adding records is slow on my laptop. What settings or habits would make it lighter and faster?
I run AI helpers on several different machines. How do I make sure two of them never work on the same piece of work at once, and that all machines agree on who has it?
I want to run a group of cooperating AI helpers in the cloud instead of on my laptop. It should grow automatically with the load and come with ready-made setups for common jobs.

Our repo's bug tracker is flooded with reports nobody has tagged, and many are repeats of each other. I'd like something to sort them, suggest tags and priorities, and merge the repeats automatically.
I want an automatic security check of our code repository that also checks compliance and opens tickets for any problems it finds, so I don't have to review everything by hand.
My AI agent's long-term memory store is eating a lot of RAM on my laptop and lookups feel slow. What settings should I change to shrink it and speed up retrieval?
My similarity search over stored text embeddings is using too much RAM on my laptop. How can I shrink the memory footprint without switching to a different database?
I'm about to share an app template I built so other people can install it from a public catalog. What should I include so it's easy for them to set up and trust?
I want to run many AI helpers together without buying my own machines. They should scale up on their own, start from ready-made setups, and let me watch what they're doing live.

I'm letting an AI assistant triage issues and comments on my public repository. How do I stop strangers from sneaking instructions or harmful shell commands into their posts and having the assistant act on them?

Before shipping a new version, I'd like to automatically build a sorted list of what changed since the last release from merged pull requests and commits. It should also include upgrade instructions for users.
When an AI assistant edits my code, I want bad edits undone on their own if they don't pass quality and safety checks. Is that possible, and what's actually working today?
I want to cryptographically sign our project's security manifest so outsiders can confirm it hasn't been altered. What kind of private key do I have to provide, and where does it go?

All our automated tests and type checks pass, yet people still hit install failures on newer runtimes and odd flag-parsing bugs. Why is that happening, and what kind of extra checking would catch these problems?
I added a new tool to one of the add-ons and I want to be sure its description will pass the automated build checks before I open a pull request. What do those checks require?
I started a remotely hosted AI assistant session to do a task, and it's finished now. How do I shut it down properly so it doesn't keep charging me?
I want to run an AI helper in an isolated sandbox so it can't touch my real machine. How do I start one, send it requests, give it specific abilities, and let it work with files there?
I have a slightly different version of the command-line tool than the add-on expects. How can I quickly confirm the add-on still works properly with what I've installed?
I want my AI coding assistant to remember facts between sessions, sorted into short-term versus long-term kinds, and then pull them back later just by asking a question.
I want my AI coding assistant to keep working through a checklist of tasks by itself, round after round, without me typing a prompt every time. Is there a way to set that up?
I want agents on two different computers to share a message board. I don't want a machine I don't trust to be able to slip in fake or corrupted posts. How does exchanging messages work?
My bot reads random web pages and passes the text to a language model. I'm worried a page could contain hidden text telling the model to act differently. Can that be caught first?
I want an AI helper to type my details into website sign-up forms for me. The forms include personal info like my email and phone, and I don't want those values saved in any logs or history.

I'm automating a website where the button names and page layout keep changing, so my scripts break. Can I just describe in plain words what to click? And when is that a bad idea because of speed or cost?
I'm automating clicks on a website and want a replayable log of every action I take, so I can see later exactly what happened at each point. How do I record that?
I recorded two automated website test runs and want to find where they went differently, both in how the pages looked and in their page structure. How can I compare them step by step?
I want automated checks of my web app in a real browser that also catch visual changes. I'd like to compare each new run with an earlier good run to see what looks different.
I'd like to find out if a smaller, cheaper AI model would cost me less than the top model for my usual coding jobs before I switch. How can I compare them on real tasks?
My spending on AI coding sessions seems to be climbing fast. How can I group costs by day over the last couple of weeks and have a script fail when today's spend jumps well above normal?
I'd like to know how much money I actually saved by using cheaper AI models. What would my past sessions have cost if everything had run on a more expensive model?
I'd like my build pipeline to fail automatically if our AI model spending jumps too much compared to an earlier snapshot, either by percentage or by dollar amount, and to show which models caused it.
I want a single spending check for my AI usage that fails my build pipeline if any one budget problem shows up, and gives me a quick pass/fail summary. How do I set that up?
My last AI coding chat was surprisingly expensive. How can I see which individual replies cost the most, and whether one of them was way out of line compared to the rest?
I'd like to set up a reusable way of reasoning for my autonomous agents, run it, see how well it works, and then pass the good ones to other agents. What's the process?
I design software around business domains. How can I save my domain model templates and business event names once and reuse them across several different projects?

My TypeScript codebase is split into separate business areas. I want to find places where one area reaches straight into another area's internal model code instead of going through its public entry point.
Our AI assistants hand work to assistants run by other teams, and sometimes they end up passing tasks back and forth forever, which burns money. How can I set a hard limit on this?

Given someone's online handle, I want to gather everything public about them: their repos, related people, and links. I'd like a readable report with a relationship diagram, plus a data file I can reuse.
My AI assistant collected lots of notes while researching a question, and some of them contradict each other. How can I turn them into one report that rates how trustworthy each claim is?
My AI helper has picked up useful habits while working on one repository. How can I reuse what it learned in another project, or on my other computer?
I want my team of AI agents to get better at working together by learning from how past tasks went, including whether each one succeeded. What steps do I follow?

We record architecture decisions in documents. When reviewing a code change, I want to automatically flag code that contradicts or relies on outdated decisions, and get a risk score and suggested reviewers.
I have a network of linked facts about people and things. Starting from one name, I want to follow its links a few hops out and see the most relevant chains of connections, with a short summary.
If I skip installing an optional add-on package, will the plugin's scripts crash or break my build? I'd like to keep my install small and leave out extra dependencies.
I ran a health check on my agent setup a while ago. Now I want to know how much the project has changed since then, and get warned if the difference is big.
I want my automated build checks to fail whenever a code repository's assessed danger level goes past a limit I choose. Can a repo analysis produce that kind of pass/fail?
Before I let a system automatically tune my AI prompts, I want to know roughly how much the run will cost me. I don't want to actually call any paid models yet.
I want AI agents to generate songs for me, but my laptop has no graphics card. Can the heavy work run somewhere else, and what access credentials do I need?
I asked my assistant to make an AI song, and after waiting several minutes it only said it failed. Did I describe the song badly, or should I just try again?
I made a song with an AI music service and want to know whether separate instrument tracks or a MIDI version are ready yet. I'd rather not waste requests on details that never change.
A job split across several AI agents is running slowly. I want to see which step took the longest and where time was spent waiting doing nothing, so I know what to fix first.

I want to build my own add-on for this AI agent tool, but I don't know what folders and files it needs. Is there a quick way to generate the starting layout and check that my files are set up correctly?
My coding assistant keeps lots of little markdown note files across different projects. I want to search them all by meaning, not by exact words, and I don't want duplicate notes piling up.
I want to turn chunks of text into numeric vectors for similarity search, save the result to a file, and process a whole folder of documents. How do I do that?
I have text embeddings for items in a tree-shaped category system. I want distances between them to reflect how deep the items sit in that tree. How do I transform and compare the vectors?
When I close my AI agent work for the day, I lose everything it was doing. I'd like to save where I left off and continue from that exact point tomorrow.

I want a really thorough check of my code project for known published vulnerabilities, plus advice on fixing whatever it finds. Ideally I could pick how intensive the check is, from a light pass to an in-depth one.
The first time I try to start this agent tool inside my coding assistant, it times out and none of its tools show up. Is there a smaller version that downloads quickly so startup doesn't fail?
I'd like an AI partner to code with me while I fix bugs in Python. I want it to review my code as I go and run the tests after every change I make. How do I set that up?
I'm about to share a project template I built on an online marketplace so others can use it. What should I include so people can set it up, trust it, and upgrade it later?
I want several AI helpers to work in sequence, with each one getting the full result of the one before it. Can I write my own series of prompts, or use ready-made sequences?
When an AI assistant edits my code, I'd like bad edits undone on their own if they don't pass quality checks. Is that possible, and how much of it really works today versus being planned?
I'm building a set of sample requests to check whether my system sends each task to the right helper. How do I mark tricky examples where obvious words would mislead a simple matcher?

I only want the lightweight version of this agent toolkit inside my AI coding assistant: just the extra chat commands. I don't want to install a full command-line setup. How do I add it and choose the pieces I need?
I'm writing small automation scripts for my project's tooling. What rules should they follow so rerunning them is harmless, they stay quick, and editing settings files never corrupts them?
I plugged a small edge hardware box into my laptop with a cable. Which address do I use to talk to it, and how do I get permission to write data to it instead of only reading?
I'm checking whether some AI-generated text carries a hidden mark, but a short code snippet shows no signal at all. Is the check broken, or is something else going on?
I have to review supplier agreements without a lawyer. I want to pull out the important sections, spot risky terms, track deadlines we owe, and check them against our preferred negotiating stance.
Some pages in my app load slowly, and I suspect the database is doing too many small lookups or is missing indexes. Is there something that can spot these problems for me automatically?
I'm letting outside users submit optimization jobs to my service. I'm worried someone will send an enormous or malicious problem that hogs memory or runs forever. What protections are built in?
Some of our automated checks pass one run and fail the next without any code changes. I want to find which ones are unreliable and understand why, and run the likely-failing ones first.
Several automated agents have to agree on decisions, but some of them might be compromised and lie on purpose or flood the others with requests. How do I get agreement that still holds up?
I'm setting up a group of cooperating AI helpers. How do I make sure their shared coordination state survives between runs, and can they open and control several shell windows at once?
The long-term memory store for my AI assistant uses too much RAM, and adding records one at a time is painfully slow. What settings or habits would shrink memory use and speed up writes and lookups?
My collection of embeddings uses too much RAM on a small machine, and loading lots of records one at a time takes forever. How can I shrink memory use and speed up big loads?
I'm about to share a reusable project template so other people can deploy it. What should I include so it's easy to set up, test, upgrade and trust?
Before launch I need to stress-test our vector database with a huge amount of traffic coming from many cloud regions. I also want automatic checks that we meet our uptime and tail-latency promises.
I've set up performance tests for a graph database. How do I tell whether everything is actually working as intended, and what results should I expect to see before trusting them?
I'm splitting a large graph across hundreds of small sandboxed workers, and each worker only gets 64KB of memory. How much memory does each worker's piece of the graph and its bookkeeping use?

I'm studying the idea that time emerges from entanglement. Starting from a completely static joint state of a clock and a system, I want to numerically show ordinary quantum evolution appearing, and check it against a regular propagator.
My team's AI assistants will send notes to a shared knowledge service. How do I stop email addresses, IP addresses or secret keys from leaking into it, and can I protect the stored data further?

I want similarity search results to feed into a brain-inspired, event-driven network. The best matches should win out over the others and connections should keep learning, so I can eventually run it on neuromorphic chips.

My automated trading system keeps updating its model even when its parameters start drifting unpredictably. I want updates blocked automatically once that drift gets too large. What mechanism handles that?

From the terminal, I want to try out and compare how fast different kinds of attention layers run, like multi-head or flash. Later I'd like to offer the same computation to other apps over a web interface.

I'm building a web app in TypeScript. I need transformer-style attention that handles tree-shaped or nested data well, plus a lighter option that saves memory on long inputs, all running in JavaScript rather than on a Python server.
I need to measure tail response times and RAM use of my similarity search on well-known public datasets, compare it with other systems, and export the results to a spreadsheet.
Each user may only see some of the documents in my similarity search. Filtering results after the search is slow. Is there a quicker way that still returns the right top matches?
I changed how embeddings get compressed to fewer bits. Where are the checks that decompressing gives back close-enough values and that distances between compressed items are still right?

Our database lookups slow down unpredictably as usage changes. Is there something that watches real runs, figures out what speeds them up, and changes its approach automatically instead of relying on fixed hand-written tuning rules?
I'm building a web app and want to store and query linked data directly in the user's browser, with no backend server. Heavy queries should run in the background so the page doesn't freeze.
I want to produce text embeddings on a Raspberry Pi 5 right now, but I don't have the accelerator's vendor runtime set up. Can I run it on the regular processor?

I'm running text embeddings on a Raspberry Pi 5 with an AI accelerator add-on. If the compiled model file for the accelerator goes missing, I want it to keep working on the plain processor without redeploying.

I need to keep finding the weakest set of links in a large network whose connections change all the time. I want exact answers after each change, not approximate ones, and I don't want to recompute from scratch.
My JavaScript backend's similarity search over embeddings is too slow and uses a lot of memory. I'd like a much faster option I can call from my server code that also compresses the stored data.

I want to run transformer attention directly on data stored in my relational database, through plain queries, without exporting it. It also shouldn't eat too much memory on long sequences. Is that possible?

I already keep my data in a relational database. I'd like to model how records are linked, find the quickest route between two of them, and ask questions in a standard graph query language, all without running a separate graph server.
My small wheeled robot gets 3D point readings from a depth camera. I want to quickly find which points are close to a given spot and flag things in its path, without setting up a heavy framework.
My iterative solver for large sparse linear systems spends most of its time multiplying the matrix by a vector. How can I avoid paying for a safety check on every element and still stay correct?
I'm building a tiny kernel for 64-bit ARM with no operating system underneath. Where do I change the memory layout, and how do I build it and run it in an emulator?
Why would a normal desktop or server OS be a poor foundation for running autonomous AI agents, and what would such agents need instead?
I have a big collection of about a million embeddings. I want several slightly edited variants of it without copying hundreds of megabytes each time. How can I keep just the changes?
From my Node app, I want to keep embeddings in a single file, find the closest ones to a query, and filter by field conditions like ranges. It also shouldn't lose data if the process crashes.

I'd like to ship one data file that also carries its own runnable code, so it can run in a web browser and also inside a secure hardware enclave or a lightweight VM. Is that possible, and how fast does it start up?
I want to run the automated tests for a desktop reader app on a headless CI machine. I don't want to install any of the GUI or browser-engine system libraries there. Is that possible?

For research, I want to simulate a water-bath scanner where a circle of ultrasound sensors surrounds a body, rebuild sound-speed and attenuation maps, and label tissue types. I have no real scanner hardware.

My embeddings change only slightly each time, but I resend the whole thing on every update, which wastes network traffic. I'd also like to see what the data looked like at an earlier time. What can do that?
Whenever my AI coding assistant edits files, I want formatting and linting to run automatically. I also want it to remember decisions from one session to the next.

Our skin clinic wants software that classifies mole images taken with a handheld dermatology scope, gets better with every case, and stays within US patient-privacy rules. Is there anything like that?

My AI agents constantly produce new embeddings very fast. The similarity search index I use either blocks while inserting or gets worse over time. How can I take in a nonstop stream of inserts and still keep search quality good?
My clustered similarity search keeps missing good matches that sit near the edges between groups. How can I recover them without checking more groups per query, if I can accept using extra storage?

My similarity search over embeddings misses too many true matches, and I can't tell how wide the search should be. I want roughly 90% accuracy without making each lookup much slower. What should I use?
My chatbot's saved memories have grown to thousands of entries, and checking every one on each lookup is getting slow. How can I speed up lookups, and how much accuracy would I lose?

When my similarity search service returns nearest-neighbor matches, I want clients to be able to confirm that the result lists came from me and weren't altered. Ideally one signature should cover a whole batch of queries.

As new memories stream into my assistant, I sort them into groups. Deciding whether each one joins an existing group or starts a new one, based only on distance to the closest group center, gives messy groups. Is there a better rule?

An auditor wants to prove our search index was really in a certain state at some point. They don't have a receipt for any specific query, and replaying the entire history of writes is too slow. What's a cheaper way?

Our AI agent's memory audit log only uses plain hash chaining. Someone who edits an entry and recomputes every later hash could fool it. How can I add real cryptographic signatures without pulling in new libraries?

My knowledge base only records simple 'X is a kind of Y' facts. I'd like an agent to check those facts against live web search on its own, correct the wrong ones, and add richer relationships between concepts.
Is it worth putting effort into the tooling and loop around my coding assistant instead of just switching to a newer model? I'd like evidence on how much it actually helps.
I've now produced a set of example training records. What should I do next to actually adapt a language model with them, and can I use whatever machine learning library I already like?
I'd like to look inside a published JavaScript library's shipped code, make it readable, and break it into pieces. I want to do this entirely from a web page without installing anything.
I want to reuse what a system learned in one subject area for a different one. It should pick whichever route has worked best before, and each step of the move should be checked so it's reliable.
When I keep training my model on new tasks, it loses what it learned earlier. I need a way for it to keep learning over time without wiping out its older skills.
My data has links that join groups of several items at once, not just pairs. I want an efficient way to count the separate clusters and cycles in that structure to summarize its shape.
I want a web page to remember items as embeddings, record when each one happened and what caused what, and later find similar ones. Everything should run inside the user's browser with no backend.

I'm exploring whether repeating physical oscillations could explain how the brain holds short-term memories. Is there a written survey that covers the physics and the neuroscience, such as rhythmic firing and neurons that track elapsed time?
I'm reading about a theory that measures consciousness as a single number. I'd like background reading on why that number is so expensive to calculate for larger systems. Where should I start?
Before I trust a distributed memory setup, I want to see tests showing that nodes can merge their states without conflicts and keep working when the network gets split. Where would I find those?
I'd like to experiment from JavaScript with brain-inspired neurons that fire in pulses and learn without labels, but plain JS is far too slow. Is there a faster option?
I have scanned research papers full of formulas and diagrams, and normal text-recognition tools mangle the math. I'd like a fast, reliable tool built for reading STEM content.
On my Windows 64-bit machine, a compiled add-on for my JavaScript project won't load. The error says a system library is missing. What do I install to fix it?

When I search for similar items but also require a strict attribute filter that only about one percent of records match, I get almost no results back. How can I keep results accurate with such narrow filters?
I want to test several chatbot providers side by side on the same task and have my prompts tuned automatically over a few rounds, while keeping track of what I'm spending.
I'm testing a system where many AI workers split up jobs, vote, and sometimes crash and restart. I need believable fake data covering those situations so I don't have to run a real fleet.
I want to tune prompts for several different AI chat providers at once and compare how well each does. I also need to keep spending under a fixed budget. What tool can do this?
We expect big traffic spikes during planned events. I want capacity added before the spikes hit, and also in response to live load, without going over our spending limit on Google's cloud.

I have a graph of facts like who works where and want to guess missing connections. The model should stay compact and support fast similarity lookups. Some facts only follow from linking two relations together.

I'm putting a sensor-reading model on a battery-powered device. It has to handle time-based signals, use very little power, and keep adapting as data streams in, without being retrained on batches. What kind of network should I look at?

I'm feeding lab results and scan data into an automated health analysis tool. How do I make sure the outside records can't push the system into declaring a diagnosis on its own, and that sensitive test results still get a person's review?
I want my assistant bots to remember things between conversations, but the data has to stay on my own machine and not go to a cloud provider. Can the memory lookup work completely offline?
I'm about to write a few small automation scripts for this project's assistant tooling. What house rules should they follow so they're safe, quick, and don't break config data when run again?

When I publish a new version of my code, I'd like the list of what changed to be written for me from the merged pull requests and commits. It should be sorted into categories and include upgrade notes.
When I open a code change request on my hosted repository, I want automated helpers to check it for style, tests, security and documentation before anyone merges it. How can I set that up?
When several AI helpers work on my code, I want tasks assigned automatically, code tidied after each change, and context remembered between work sessions. What can set that up for me?
I'm helping rebuild the core business logic layer and want to know what quality bar counts as done: how much testing, how strict the typing, and how fast and lean it should run.
AI helpers sometimes change my code in ways that break things. I want each change given a reliability score and undone automatically if it doesn't meet a quality bar.

My model that estimates body position from wireless signals works in the lab but is nearly useless in a customer's house. Should I gather data from lots more people, or is there a cheaper fix at install time?
I'm new and trying to read this project's design write-ups, but they keep using structured section types I don't understand. What does each kind of section describe, so I can follow along?

I'm worried that someone nearby could passively pick up my home wireless traffic and figure out who is in the house. Is there a way to block that without slowing down my internet or jamming the signal?
I want to run the whole project's automated tests inside a Linux container that has no graphical desktop libraries installed. One part keeps failing to build. How do I run everything else?

I want smart automated assistants that watch the home sensing events and reason about them, e.g. notice nobody has been in the kitchen for hours with an appliance left on and alert a caregiver, without building an agent runtime myself.
I'm adding a custom page to the smart-home web dashboard and want it to match the existing look exactly: colors, fonts and icons. What values should I use, and do I need to support a bright theme?

My home automation dashboard shows the presence sensors with long hardware-address names that I can't make sense of. How can I give them readable names like the bedroom one without breaking how they get picked up?
Can I get a rough blood pressure reading for someone without putting a cuff or anything else on their body? I only want to use their heart rhythm picked up from across the room.

I'm sensing people using wireless signal readings. How do I work out which frequency channels actually carry useful information, and how do I tell when the readings from several radio links can't be trusted?
On a tight budget, I only want to use basic signal strength readings to see whether animals or people are in a barn and how many. Could that cheap setup also measure breathing?
If the system recognises the same person as they move from room to room, what stops that identity data being misused? I want to keep it private and only store it if people agree.

I have a small microcontroller board sending radio measurements over the network, and I'd like my 3D browser scene to animate from them live. How do I get that data into the web page, and what happens when the board is offline?
The body outline I estimate from wireless signals never lines up with the person on my laptop webcam. I trained it using video from another camera. How can I get the stick figure to match?
Could I use a cheap hobby microcontroller board to scramble its own wireless feedback so outsiders can't fingerprint the people in my home, or do I need other hardware?

I want to stop anyone from detecting movement in my home through my wifi signals, using the open-source firmware already on my router. Can it fully scramble the signal, or do I need different hardware?

I've put the wireless sensor in a new bedroom and want it to reliably tell when someone's there, how they're sitting or lying, and whether they're breathing. What setup steps get it tuned to this particular space?
I trained a model that guesses body joint positions from sensor data, and its accuracy looks decent. How do I report the score honestly so I'm not fooling myself about how good it really is?

After I upgraded my Python number-crunching libraries, the self-check that confirms the signal processing still gives identical output started failing. How do I get it to pass again without faking anything?
From my terminal, I want to sign into our cloud account and get a list of our buildings and alert records, page by page. I don't want to paste a secret key anywhere.
I'd like to automatically try out small changes to my code to make it better, but on a machine with no internet and no paid AI key. Changes must not add risky things like file or shell access.
I want my test setup to suggest improvements to its own settings, but I need to preview the changes before anything is applied. I'd also like it to pick the cheapest AI model for each step.
I'm building a phone app to capture room depth scans, but I get no depth data in the Mac simulator. I also don't want any camera pictures leaving the device. What do I need?
I use OpenAI's terminal coding assistant, not Anthropic's. Can I still use this project's ready-made workflows and project rules with it, and where do I need to put the files?
I want to record what my room normally looks like when nobody is there, then detect what has changed compared to that. The saved reference also needs to survive a reboot.
I'd like to keep an eye on my elderly dad's breathing while he's asleep in bed, using wireless signals rather than a camera. Which kind of sensing should I set up for that?
I want to quickly try the web dashboard and HTTP endpoints of this wifi sensing system without compiling any code myself. What's the fastest way to get it running locally?
I changed just one setting on my sensor board over USB, and now its other saved settings, like the wifi password, seem to have vanished. Why did that happen, and how do I avoid it?
I connected a small radar module for breathing and heart rate to my microcontroller board. Do I need extra setup so its readings get combined with the wifi-based health readings?

After updating the math libraries on my machine, I want to prove that the signal-processing results haven't quietly changed. If the check fails only because of the library update, I also need to reset the reference.
I want to track my elderly dad's breathing and heartbeat at home without putting a camera in his room. I'd like to do it from a small script and know when readings can't be trusted.

I downloaded a public academic dataset of wireless recordings labeled by which person is present. I want to convert it into training data without running any untrusted code from the archive. How do I do that?

I captured wireless traffic containing the beam-steering reports that routers send each other, and I want the actual per-subcarrier angle values rather than just totals. Can I get them, and will a newer-format capture file work?
My phone app runs in an emulator on my laptop, and the backend that streams the sensor readings runs in a container on the same machine. What address should the app point at to get live data?

I want to train a small embedding model in JavaScript using a contrastive objective. I'd also like weight decay and a learning rate that ramps up and then gradually drops. Is there a typed library with those built in?

I'm setting up a smart-home alert at a care home that should warn when a sensor's chance of recognizing specific people suddenly jumps. The automation template won't validate. Why, and is something broken?

I want my room-presence sensor to send events to my home automation hub and be found automatically on my local network. I don't want any biometric data shared, and I want logs nobody can quietly alter.
I want to count how many people are in a room from wireless signal readings. I have several sensors and need a confidence level with each estimate, not a rough guess.
On the little home sensing box, I'd like to see stick-figure body joints worked out from the wireless signals appear live on its web screen. What piece does that and how does it feed the display?
I'm writing a small script to read my smart home devices and switch them on or off over the network. It should get live updates in a browser and require a secret key. What web endpoints can I use?
I'd like to type or say plain sentences like "turn off the kitchen light" and have my self-hosted smart home understand them and do it. Is there a piece that handles understanding commands?
I want to write simple home rules like 'when the hallway sensor sees motion after dark, turn on the lamp' in plain text files. They should load on their own when the system starts.
I'm linking my DIY home gadget to the smart-home app on my phone. Where do the pairing secrets end up on disk, and could other users on the same computer read them or find the setup PIN?
I want to move my existing home automation setup, including devices and integrations, onto a new hub. I'm worried a half-finished import could wipe out files that already exist. Is that safe?

I'm building a smart home hub in a fast systems language. I need a core that stores the current status of every device and tells other parts of the program when something changes, safely across many threads.
I'm on a rescue team and want one terminal tool to run scans that find and sort people trapped after a disaster, using wireless signals. Which command should I start with?
I have several sensing nodes talking to each other, and I'd like a picture on my computer of how they're connected and whether each one is healthy, without installing extra graph software.
After an earthquake, can ordinary wireless router signals help find people buried under a fallen building? I want something I can build into our own rescue software.
